questions.q: As of which HTTP version is the Host header a mandatory request header?
choices: HTTP/1.0
HTTP/1.1
HTTP/2
HTTP/3
questions.explain: The Host header became mandatory as of HTTP/1.1.

questions.q: What does the HTTP Host header specify, and what is its purpose?
choices: The client's own IP address, so the server can reply
The domain name the client wants to access, helping identify which back-end component to route to
The preferred content language of the response
The TLS cipher suite to use for the connection
questions.explain: It specifies the domain the client wants to reach so the server/intermediary can route the request to the intended back-end component.

questions.q: Historically, routing ambiguity didn't exist because each IP address only hosted content for a single domain.
questions.explain: Nowadays multiple sites commonly share one IP (cloud/SaaS, CDNs), partly due to IPv4 address exhaustion, which is why the Host header is needed to disambiguate.

questions.q: What term describes multiple websites hosted on a single server, each with a different domain name but sharing a common IP address?
questions.explain: Sites hosted this way on one server are known as 'virtual hosts'; to a normal user a virtual host is often indistinguishable from a dedicated server.

questions.q: In a setup where all of a site's domains resolve to a single intermediary IP (e.g. a CDN, load balancer, or reverse proxy), what does the intermediary rely on to choose the correct back-end?
choices: The source TCP port
The Host header
The User-Agent string
The TLS session ID
questions.explain: Like virtual hosting, routing via an intermediary relies on the Host header to specify the intended recipient back-end.

questions.q: Why do off-the-shelf web applications sometimes read the current domain from the Host header?
choices: To validate the user's session cookie
They often don't know which domain they're deployed on, so they use it to build absolute URLs (e.g. links in emails)
To compress the response body
To decide which database shard to query by default
questions.explain: Unless the domain is set in config, apps may pull it from the Host header to generate absolute URLs such as those in emails.

questions.q: What is a 'Host header injection' attack?
choices: Guessing valid Host values with a wordlist
Injecting a harmful payload directly into the Host header that a site handles unsafely
Forcing a victim's browser to send a forged Host header
Overflowing the server's header parser buffer
questions.explain: When a server implicitly trusts the Host header and fails to validate/escape it, an attacker can inject a payload directly into it to manipulate server-side behavior.

questions.q: Which of the following are listed as vulnerabilities the Host header can be a vector for? (Select all that apply)
choices: Web cache poisoning
Business logic flaws in specific functionality
Routing-based SSRF
Classic server-side vulnerabilities such as SQL injection
Buffer overflow in the TCP/IP stack
questions.explain: The Host header is cited as a potential vector for web cache poisoning, business logic flaws, routing-based SSRF, and classic server-side bugs like SQL injection.

questions.q: Host header vulnerabilities typically arise from the flawed assumption that the header is NOT user controllable.
questions.explain: This implicit trust leads to inadequate validation/escaping, even though an attacker can easily modify the header with tools like Burp Proxy.

questions.q: Many Host header vulnerabilities arise from insecure configuration of infrastructure components rather than from insecure coding.
questions.explain: Integrating third-party technologies without understanding their configuration options and security implications is a common root cause.

questions.q: Even when the Host header itself is handled securely, how can its value sometimes still be overridden?
choices: By sending the request over HTTP/2 only
By injecting other headers (e.g. X-Forwarded-Host) that are supported by default
By using a longer URL path
By omitting the Host header entirely
questions.explain: Depending on server configuration, headers like X-Forwarded-Host can override the Host; owners often don't realize such headers are supported by default.

questions.q: Why are reflected client-side vulnerabilities such as XSS, when caused by the Host header, typically NOT directly exploitable?
choices: Browsers HTML-encode all Host values automatically
There is no way for an attacker to force a victim's browser to issue an incorrect Host in a useful manner
The Host header is always stripped by the server
XSS cannot occur in server-rendered markup
questions.explain: An attacker can't make the victim's own browser send a malicious Host, so the reflection isn't directly exploitable, unless a cache can be poisoned to store it.

questions.q: Which tool accurately maintains the separation between the Host header and the target IP address, letting you send an arbitrary Host while still reaching the intended target?
choices: curl
Burp Suite
nmap
Wireshark
questions.explain: Some proxies derive the target IP from the Host header; Burp Suite keeps them separate so you can supply any arbitrary or malformed Host and still reach the target.

questions.q: What two-word error message (shown as 'Invalid ___ ___') might a front-end or load balancer return when it can't route a request whose Host you modified?
questions.explain: Tampering with the Host often means the front-end doesn't know where to forward the request, producing an 'Invalid Host header' error of some kind.

questions.q: Some websites validate the Host header by checking that it matches what from the TLS handshake?
choices: The certificate serial number
The SNI
The cipher suite
The session ticket
questions.explain: Matching the Host against the SNI from the TLS handshake is one defense, but it doesn't necessarily make a site immune to Host header attacks.

questions.q: What is the de facto standard HTTP header used to override/carry the original Host value, often referred to by frameworks instead of the Host header?
questions.explain: Front ends inject X-Forwarded-Host with the client's original Host; many frameworks prefer it, so it can be used to inject input while bypassing Host validation.

questions.q: Besides X-Forwarded-Host, which headers are listed as serving a similar override purpose? (Select all that apply)
choices: X-Host
X-Forwarded-Server
X-HTTP-Host-Override
Forwarded
X-Real-IP
questions.explain: X-Host, X-Forwarded-Server, X-HTTP-Host-Override, and Forwarded are all named as alternatives that can override the Host.

questions.q: When injecting duplicate Host headers or supplying an absolute URL in the request line, what are you fundamentally trying to exploit?
choices: A buffer overflow in the parser
A discrepancy where different systems (e.g. front-end vs back-end) disagree about which value is the correct Host
A timing side channel
A weakness in the TLS handshake
questions.explain: These 'ambiguous request' techniques exploit discrepancies in how the validating component and the vulnerable component each retrieve the Host.

questions.q: How can a reflected, 'useless' Host header vulnerability be turned into a dangerous, stored one that affects other users?
choices: By brute-forcing the victim's session token
By poisoning a web cache so it serves the malicious response to other users
By forcing the victim's browser to resend the request
By exploiting a TLS downgrade
questions.explain: If the target uses a web cache, you can elicit a reflected-payload response and get it cached so it is served to subsequent visitors.

questions.q: Standalone caches typically include the Host header in the cache key, so Host-based cache poisoning usually works best against integrated, application-level caches.
questions.explain: Because standalone caches key on the Host, the approach works best on integrated application-level caches, though earlier ambiguous-request techniques can sometimes poison standalone caches too.

questions.q: In the malformed request line 'GET @private-intranet/example HTTP/1.1', a proxy builds the URL http://backend-server@private-intranet/example. How do most HTTP libraries interpret that?
choices: As a request to backend-server with path @private-intranet
As a request to private-intranet with the username backend-server
As an invalid URL that is rejected
As a request to the literal host 'backend-server@private-intranet'
questions.explain: The '@' makes 'backend-server' be read as userinfo, so the request is routed to private-intranet, enabling routing-based SSRF via a malformed request line.

questions.q: What is the goal of virtual host brute-forcing?
choices: Cracking the server's TLS private key
Accessing internal or hidden websites on a server by guessing their hostnames
Exhausting the server's connection pool
Flooding the DNS resolver with queries
questions.explain: An attacker can reach any virtual host on a server they can connect to if they guess the hostname, e.g. brute-forcing candidate subdomains, even when the site has no public DNS record.

questions.q: Which Burp tool helps confirm a routing-based SSRF by receiving a DNS lookup when you supply its domain in the Host header?
choices: Burp Intruder
Burp Collaborator
Burp Decoder
Param Miner
questions.explain: If supplying your Burp Collaborator domain in the Host triggers a DNS lookup from the target or an in-path system, you may be able to route requests to arbitrary domains.

questions.q: In CIDR notation 192.168.0.0/16, how many bits from the start of the address are fixed for the entire range?
questions.explain: The number after the slash is the count of fixed leading bits; /16 fixes the first two octets (192.168), leaving the rest to vary.

questions.q: What dangerous assumption underlies a connection state attack against the Host header?
choices: That TLS is always terminated at the back-end
That certain properties like the Host header are identical for every HTTP/1.1 request sent over the same reused connection
That the client always uses HTTP/2
That the cache never stores error responses
questions.explain: Servers that validate only the first request on a connection, or reverse proxies that route all requests on a connection to the first request's host, can be abused; a browser wouldn't vary the Host, but Burp Repeater can.

questions.q: What is password reset poisoning?
choices: Flooding a user with reset emails until their account locks
Manipulating a site into generating a reset link that points to an attacker-controlled domain, to steal the reset token
Guessing a user's reset token by brute force
Corrupting the password database so resets fail
questions.explain: By controlling the domain in the generated reset link (via the Host header), the attacker can capture the victim's valid reset token and take over the account.

questions.q: In a typical password reset flow, how is the unique, high-entropy reset token delivered to the user?
choices: As a query parameter in a reset link emailed to the user
As an SMS one-time code
Embedded in a session cookie
Displayed on screen immediately after the request
questions.explain: The token is associated with the account on the back-end and included as a query parameter in the reset URL sent by email, e.g. /reset?token=...

questions.q: In a password reset poisoning attack, the victim receives a genuine reset email from the real website containing a valid token, but the link's domain points to the attacker.
questions.explain: The email is legitimate and carries a working token; only the host in the URL has been poisoned to point at the attacker's server.

questions.q: In the worked example, what attacker-controlled domain is injected via the Host header so the reset link becomes https://<domain>/reset?token=...?
questions.explain: The example uses evil-user.net as the attacker's domain in the poisoned reset link.

questions.q: Besides the victim clicking it, how else might a poisoned reset link deliver the token to the attacker's server?
choices: The token expires and auto-submits
The link being fetched automatically by something like an antivirus scanner
The browser pre-rendering the inbox
The mail server rewriting all links
questions.explain: The token can leak if the link is fetched in some other way, for example by an antivirus scanner that follows links.

questions.q: If you can't control the reset link itself, what else can the Host header sometimes allow in sensitive emails (noting that email clients typically don't run JavaScript)?
choices: Arbitrary JavaScript execution in the client
HTML injection, enabling techniques like dangling markup attacks
Direct database access
Rewriting the email's From address
questions.explain: The Host header can be used to inject HTML into emails; since clients don't execute JS, dangling markup and similar HTML injection techniques are the relevant threat.

questions.q: What is described as the simplest approach to prevent HTTP Host header attacks?
choices: Block all requests that lack a Host header
Avoid using the Host header in server-side code, using relative URLs where possible
Rotate reset tokens every minute
Terminate TLS at the back-end
questions.explain: Checking whether each URL really needs to be absolute and preferring relative URLs avoids relying on the Host header, which especially helps against web cache poisoning.

questions.q: When you must use absolute URLs, what does the guidance recommend?
choices: Derive the domain from the first request on each connection
Require the current domain to be set in a configuration file and use that value instead of the Host header
Trust X-Forwarded-Host over Host
Hash the Host header before use
questions.explain: Referring to a manually configured domain instead of the Host header eliminates threats such as password reset poisoning.

questions.q: What Django settings option is given as an example for whitelisting permitted hosts?
questions.explain: Django's ALLOWED_HOSTS lets you validate the Host against a whitelist of permitted domains.

questions.q: You should make sure your application does not support Host-override headers such as X-Forwarded-Host, remembering they may be enabled by default.
questions.explain: Supporting override headers like X-Forwarded-Host (often on by default via third-party tech) can be used to construct these attacks.

questions.q: To prevent routing-based attacks on internal infrastructure, how should load balancers and reverse proxies be configured?
choices: To forward requests only to a whitelist of permitted domains
To cache every response for one hour
To accept duplicate Host headers
To strip the request line's path
questions.explain: Forwarding only to a whitelist of permitted domains stops intermediaries from being tricked into routing to arbitrary internal systems.

questions.q: When using virtual hosting, what practice should you avoid to limit Host header manipulation risk?
choices: Serving static assets from a CDN
Hosting internal-only websites on the same server as public-facing content
Using HTTPS for all virtual hosts
Giving each virtual host its own TLS certificate
questions.explain: Co-hosting internal-only apps with public content lets attackers reach internal domains via Host header manipulation, so keep them separate.
